newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan pension body seeks recourse if insurers fail.
newsitem.headline: Japan pension body seeks recourse if insurers fail.

text.p: Japan's Pension Welfare Service Public Corp (Nempuku) urged Japan's life insurance industry organisation to allow rapid annulment of investment contracts with life insurers that fail, a Nempuku official said on Friday.
The request, made in a letter to the Life Insurance Association of Japan, was prompted by last week's failure of Nissan Mutual Life Insurance Co, the official told Reuters.

Nempuku, which is affiliated with the health ministry, also sent a letter to Nissan Life indicating its intention to annul its investment management contract with the medium-sized insurer, the official said.
Nempuku manages about 22 trillion yen worth of pension funds through trust banks, life insurance companies and investment management companies.
Sixteen life insurers, including Nissan Life, manage about three trillion yen worth of funds on behalf of the public fund body.

"We are fully aware that our contract with Nissan Life cannot be annulled right away due to the Ministry of Finance's (MOF) orders. But we expressed our intention (to annul our investment contract) in order to fulfil our responsibilities as a trustee of public funds," the official said.
MOF said in a statement last Friday that it ordered Nissan Life to halt all operations except for servicing current customers.
Under MOF's orders, existing contracts cannot be annulled until a new company taking over Nissan Life's business is set up.

All funds managed by life insurers for Nempuku are under special accounts, which differ from general accounts in that they have no guaranteed rates of return. General accounts are currently guaranteed a minimum 2.5 percent rate of return.
In addition, unlike general accounts, which are pooled, special accounts are managed separately from other accounts.

Fearing that money in special accounts might be used to cover losses in other accounts, Nempuku in its letter urged life insurers to respect the separation between general accounts and special accounts.
"The special accounts we have with insurers belong only to us. There should not be any transfer of money to other accounts," the official said.

"If we, as a holder of special accounts, are placed in a disadvantageous position in the event of premium refunds, we may have to review whether special accounts are appropriate as an investment vehicle for public pension funds," the official said.
Asked about the possibility of reviewing contracts with life insurers, the official said: "At this point, we do not know how they will respond to our requests."
The body has asked the association to respond to its letter by May 10.
